items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 4: AI literacy
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.
items.why: Source of the quotation. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). The page shows the amended wording (measures to support the development of AI literacy; no guaranteed level) under 'AMENDED' labels, while its banner still says the text has not yet been updated for the Digital Omnibus: both are recorded in the log. Applies to providers and deployers within the Act's scope, not to UK organisations generally. Year is the year of the amendment shown.

items.title: Timeline for the Implementation of the EU AI Act
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: The timeline takes into account the AI Act amendments introduced by Digital Omnibus on AI.
items.why: Source of the dates in the brief: AI literacy applies from 2 February 2025; enforcement of AI literacy at national level starts 2 August 2026. A Commission summary, not the legal text.

items.title: AI Literacy - Questions & Answers
items.locator: Answers on measuring knowledge, on whether training is mandatory, on 'other persons', and on enforcement
items.quote: Article 4 of the AI Act does not entail an obligation to measure the knowledge of AI of employees.
items.why: The Commission's reading of the duty after the 2026 amendment: no set level and no duty to measure, but relying on the instructions for use is not enough; contractors and service providers are within 'other persons'; national market surveillance authorities enforce. The page's opening line still describes the pre-amendment wording ('sufficient level'), and it gives the enforcement start as both 2 and 3 August 2026: see the log. Not binding.

items.title: AI skills for life and work: employer survey findings
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (research by Ipsos)
items.locator: Key findings; section 5, Figure 5.6; methodology (sample size 801, fieldwork 19 March to 7 June 2024)
items.quote: 11% of employers have had staff undertake training on AI in the last 12 months.
items.why: Source of the figure. A telephone and online survey of 801 UK employers; fieldwork was in 2024 although publication was in January 2026, so the figure is dated. The report states it does not represent government views or policy. Also reports that half of employers were unsure what training is relevant.

items.title: Research evidence, analysis and methodology: What works for AI upskilling in the UK
items.publisher: Skills England (author: Dr Nisreen Ameen, Royal Holloway, University of London)
items.quote: The evidence includes 23 workshops, 10 case studies and a survey of 536 responses.
items.why: The most recent UK official evidence on what makes workplace AI training effective, with a set of six training principles and employer guidance. Co-developed with Skills England; the opinions are the author's. The survey sample was recruited through an online crowdsourcing platform, so its percentages are not used in the brief.

items.title: One third of employers think AI will increase productivity
items.locator: 'Some top tips for employers from Acas on the use of AI at work'
items.quote: AI should be cited when used and staff may require training on how to get the best outputs.
items.why: Acas advice to employers on AI at work, issued with a survey of 1,015 senior decision makers: clear policies, consultation, outputs checked for accuracy, tone and bias, and training. Advice in a news release, not a statutory code. No fuller Acas guidance page on AI was found on the date checked.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 9: You have the skills and expertise needed to implement and use AI solutions
items.quote: You should understand the technical and ethical requirements for using AI tools and have them in place within your team.
items.why: The UK government's own standard for its staff: teams, decision makers and senior responsible owners are expected to gain AI skills. Applies to government departments and public sector organisations, not to companies; cited as a UK benchmark.

items.title: AI Opportunities Action Plan
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: Government should ensure there are sufficient opportunities for workers to reskill
items.why: UK policy on AI skills is delivered through programmes and recommendations, not a duty on employers: the plan asks government to size the skills gap and make lifelong skills provision ready for AI. Read to confirm that no employer obligation is proposed in it.

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 2, Task 5: Prepare implementers to deploy your AI system
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: Introduction and 'Educate implementers about the strengths and limitations of AI decision-support systems'
items.quote: Your training should avoid any anthropomorphic (or human-like) portrayals of AI systems.
items.why: The regulator's account of what training for staff who act on AI output should contain: the statistical character of the systems, their limits, and the biases of over-trust and distrust. Page metadata date 19 November 2024; no 'under review' banner was seen on this page on the date checked.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: The organization’s personnel and partners receive AI risk management training to enable them to perform their
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary US framework that makes training of personnel and partners an explicit governance outcome, which matches the reach to contractors in the EU duty.
